Definition
In this lesson, you will learn about the operation of DC motors and generators.
INTRODUCTIONM
These devices are commonly found in many types of electronic equipment when motion or alternate power is required.
DC motors and DC generators are types of rotating machinery.
As an electronic technician you will be required to service equipment that uses DC motors and generators.
More and more electronic devices are using rotating machinery.
Motors drive components to produce motion and generators supply power that is not normally available.
Let's begin the lesson on DC MOTORS AND GENERATORS........................
LESSON MENU
DC MOTOR GENERATOR ACTION
All DC motors and generators -- in fact all rotating machinery -- operate on the same principle: magnetism.
DISCUSSION
The first principle of magnetism used in motors-generators is; like magnetic poles repel and unlike magnetic poles attract.
When two magnetic poles, of the same potential, are close together, the magnetic fields repel the magnets.
When two magnetic poles, of opposite potential, are close together, the magnetic fields attract the magnets.......
The second principle of magnetism used in motors and generators is that; when passing a conductor through a magnetic field an electric current is produced.........
When the conductor moves up through the magnetic field, current flow is produced......
When the conductor moves down through the magnetic field, opposite current flow is produced.
As long as these two principles are remembered, motor and generator action is simple.
Let's start with motor action..............................
GENERATORS
Basic DC motor action is based on the magnetic principle of attraction and repulsion.
The basic DC motor consists of a magnetic rotor that is free to rotate.
The rotor is connected to the output shaft, and this combination rotates on a single pivot point.
The rotor is placed between two fixed magnetic stators.
Notice the rotor and stator's magnetic poles are the same.
Since like magnetic poles repel, the rotor will rotate around the pivot.
Once the rotor and stator magnetic poles are opposite, attraction will continue the rotation.
Because unlike poles attract, when the rotor has turned 180 degrees rotation stops.
Of course, this is not continuous motion, only a rotation of
To continue the rotation, the magnetic poles of the rotor must be reversed.
Now, the rotor will rotate another 180 degrees.
As long as the magnetic poles of the rotor are reversed, the rotation will continue.
The motor action you have observed is not true motor operation because the poles of a magnet can not be changed.
The motor action you observed was used to illustrate basic motor action.

To produce actual DC motor action, the permanent magnet rotor is replaced by an electromagnetic rotor.
By applying a DC voltage, in one polarity, a North and South pole is produced.
By reversing the polarity, the North and South poles are reversed.
Reversing the polarity is accomplished by using brushes and a commutator.
The brushes are made of a soft conductive material and ride on the commutator.
The commutator is in 2 pieces, these are connected to the ends of a wire loop. The wire loop is wrapped around the rotor.
More than one loop is used in DC motors. Only one is shown for clarity.
With the DC voltage applied, the "b'' half of the rotor becomes a North pole and the "a'' half becomes a South pole.
Since the rotor and stator have like poles, the attraction and repulsion of the poles cause rotation.
Because the stator and rotor poles are opposite, rotation stops.
Due to the brushes and commutator, the poles of the rotor reverse.
Since like poles repel, the rotor continues to rotate.
The brushes and commutator again reverse the polarity.
By using brushes, a commutator, and an electromagnet rotor, true continuous DC motor action occurs.

GENERATORS
Basic DC generator action is based on the principle that by passing a conductor through a magnetic field, a current or voltage is produced.
The construction of the DC generator is almost identical to the DC motor.
The difference is that the power source is replaced with a load.
As the armature is rotated through the magnetic field of the permanent magnet stator, a current or voltage is produced.

The action of the One Loop or Two Pole DC generator produces pulsating DC voltage. The action of the One Loop or Two Pole DC generator produces pulsating DC voltage.....
When the armature is at the 0/360 degree position, the armature's motion is parallel to the magnetic field of the stator and no lines of force are cut.
Since no lines of force are cut, no voltage is produced.
As the armature rotates towards the 90 degree position movement is perpendicular to the lines of force.
The perpendicular movement of the armature cuts more and more lines of force. This action increases the voltage.
Continued rotation toward the 180 degree position causes less and less lines of force to be cut.
With no lines of force being cut at the 180 degree position, motion is again parallel to the lines of force, no voltage is produced.
As the armature continues to rotate towards 270 degrees motion becomes perpendicular with the lines of force. This motion cuts through more and more lines of force.
This action increases the voltage output.
The commutator and brushes reverse the current flow to keep the flow in the same direction through the load.
Finally, as the armature's rotation approaches the 0/360 degree position, less and less lines of force are cut and the voltage drops back to zero.
What level of voltage is produced in a DC generator when the armature movement is perpendicular to the stator field?
No voltage is produced when the armature movement is parallel to the stator field, at 0, 180, and 360 degrees.
TRY AGAIN!
To generate a smoother DC output voltage, a two loop or four pole, DC generator is used.
With Loop 1 and Loop 2 ninety degrees apart, the combined output through the commutator produces a smoother DC output voltage.
Note that most commercial DC generators use from 12 to 24 loops (24 to 48 poles).

The difference between a motor and a generator is the generator does not have an applied voltage to the rotor, only an output load.
Other types of DC generators use an electromagnet stator...
One configuration, called a separately excited DC generator, uses an external power source for the stator.
The other configuration, called a self excited DC generator, uses the output voltage of the generator to supply the stator voltage.

DEFINITION
RETENTIVITY - Retentivity of an electromagnet is the small amount of magnetism that remains after a magnetizing force has been removed.
This small amount of magnetism is enough to produce a small amount of output voltage when the armature begins to rotate.
The generated voltage then adds to the magnetic field of the stator producing more output voltage.
The process continues until equilibrium is reached.

The output of the photodiode as the wheel rotates, is square wave pulses with a frequency equal to the speed of the motor-generator set.
The output of the photodiode represents RPS (revolutions per second). RPS is used because frequency is in cycles per second, Hz.
The output of the photodiode is applied as a frequency to voltage (F/V) converter, U2.
If the input frequency increases, meaning RPS increased, the voltage output of U2 on pin 7 increases.
If the input frequency decreases, meaning RPS decreased, the voltage output of the F/V converter decreases.
The voltage output of the F/V converter is then applied to U1 to change the applied voltage to the motor through S2.
The voltage output of the F/V converter is then applied to U1 to change the applied voltage to the motor through S2.
OP-AMP U1 - U1 is an op-amp configured for a diference amplifier. The output is the voltage on the non-inverting input minus the voltage on the inverting input.
If the RPS increases, the voltage output of the F/V converter increases which will decrease the output voltage of U1.
The decreased output of U1 causes the motor to slow down, compensating for the increase in RPS.
If the RPS decreases, the voltage output of the F/V converter decreases which will increase the output voltage of U1.
The increased output of U1 causes the motor to speed up, compensating for the decrease in RPS.
This is automatic speed control. If no automatic speed control is needed, S2 is placed in the open position.
The other components connected to U2 scale the output voltage.

Next let's see the effects of Counter Electromotive Force, CEMF. ter electromotive force, CEMF.
Recall that CEMF is a voltage produced by a motor that opposes the applied voltage. CEMF is produced by generator action of the motor.
Since the voltage is internal to the motor, it can not be measured directly. However, you can measure the effects of CEMF by measuring the current drawn by the motor.
When a DC voltage is first applied to the motor, the rotor is not rotating and the CEMF is zero.
The current drawn equals the applied voltage (Ea) divided by the internal resistance of the rotor (Rr).
As the rotor begins to rotate, CEMF increases from 0 volts.
Now, the current equals the applied voltage (Ea) minus the CEMF voltage (Ecemf) divided by the internal resistance of the rotor (Rr).
The current flow is less since Ecemf reduces Ea. This means that the starting current of a motor is higher than the running current.

Recall that CEMF is a voltage produced by a motor that opposes the applied voltage. CEMF is produced by generator action of the motor.
Since the voltage is internal to the motor, it can not be measured directly. However, you can measure the effects of CEMF by measuring the current drawn by the motor.
When a DC voltage is first applied to the motor, the rotor is not rotating and the CEMF is zero.
The current drawn equals the applied voltage (Ea) divided by the internal resistance of the rotor (Rr).
As the rotor begins to rotate, CEMF increases from 0 volts.
Now, the current equals the applied voltage (Ea) minus the CEMF voltage (Ecemf) divided by the internal resistance of the rotor (Rr).
The current flow is less since Ecemf reduces Ea. This means that the starting current of a motor is higher than the running current.
